featured.name: Enterprise ERP V2
featured.summary: A modular ERP covering the full trading lifecycle for electronic component distributors.
featured.problem: Component distributors run on long, interlocking workflows. A customer request becomes a quotation, then a sales order, a purchase order, a shipment, an invoice and occasionally a return. Each step has its own rules, documents and permissions, and the data has to stay consistent across all of them.
responsibilities: Architecture and technical design across the core trading modules
Full-stack delivery, from data model to interface
featured.solution: A TypeScript application with a React and Next.js front end and a Node.js and Express API over Microsoft SQL Server. Each business area is a module with its own data model, validation and screens: companies and customers, inventory, quotations and RFQs, sales and purchase orders, invoices, shipping and logistics, returns and RMAs, and administration. Modules share common patterns for lists, documents, forms and permission checks, so new areas follow a familiar shape.

decisions.title: Validate at the boundary
decisions.body: Zod schemas check every request at the API edge, so business logic only ever handles well-formed data and errors are reported in one consistent way.

decisions.title: Typed data access
decisions.body: TypeORM entities describe the relational model in TypeScript, keeping the schema and the application code in step as modules grow.

decisions.title: Shared application patterns
decisions.body: Reusable building blocks for list views, document workflows and permission checks make a large surface area feel like one product and keep new modules fast to build.

decisions.title: Explicit client state
decisions.body: Redux Toolkit manages state across multi-step screens such as converting a quotation into an order, where several views depend on the same data.

tradeoffs: ORM convenience versus control: everyday work is faster with TypeORM, while heavier reporting paths need closer attention to the SQL being produced.
Shared patterns bring consistency, but they become a product in their own right and need the same care as any other module.
A broad modular system is flexible for customers, at the cost of more configuration and permissions to reason about.
outcomes: Supports day-to-day trading workflows for distribution businesses in production
Gives each workflow, from RFQ to RMA, a consistent interface and permission model
Provides the platform the other projects on this page integrate with

featured.name: Classifex
featured.summary: AI-assisted classification of electronic components into tariff and HS codes, with people in the loop.
featured.problem: Every component that crosses a border needs a tariff code. Descriptions are inconsistent, tariff schedules change, and a wrong code has a real cost. Classifying by hand is slow, and automating it blindly is risky.
responsibilities: Data model for provenance and tariff versions
featured.solution: Classifex turns component descriptions and product attributes into structured data, proposes a tariff and HS code, and sends uncertain cases to a person for review. Each suggestion records where it came from and which version of the tariff data it was made against.

decisions.title: People stay in the loop
decisions.body: The model suggests, a reviewer confirms or corrects. Classification is treated as decision support, not a replacement for judgement.

decisions.title: Confidence shapes the workflow
decisions.body: How sure the system is affects what happens next, so attention goes to the cases that need it most.

decisions.title: Provenance on every result
decisions.body: Each code carries its inputs, the model that produced it and who reviewed it, so a result can always be explained later.

decisions.title: Version-aware tariff data
decisions.body: Tariff schedules change. Results are tied to the version they were made against rather than silently drifting.

decisions.title: Benchmark before choosing
decisions.body: Candidate models are compared on the same data before any is trusted with real classifications.

tradeoffs: Sending more cases to review is safer but slower. Where to draw that line is a product decision as much as a modelling one.
Storing provenance and versions adds data-model complexity, in exchange for results that can be audited and explained.
outcomes: Under active evaluation. No accuracy figures are published yet, deliberately.
Where my engineering and research meet: calibrated confidence matters in a customs workflow just as it does on a drone.

featured.name: Ask Dashing
featured.summary: An AI assistant that helps customers find component information and get routine tasks done.
featured.problem: Many support requests were variations on the same few tasks: finding a datasheet, looking for an alternative part number, or writing a request for quotation. The answers existed, but they were spread across systems and took people time to assemble.
responsibilities: Connecting AI capabilities to existing data and workflows
Deciding where the assistant should help and where it should hand over
featured.solution: Ask Dashing combines AI-assisted retrieval with Dashing's own product information. It helps users look up component datasheets, search for alternative part numbers and draft RFQ emails, and it sits inside the existing software rather than beside it.

decisions.title: Grounded in existing data
decisions.body: Answers are built from the company's own information rather than a model's general knowledge, which keeps them relevant and checkable.

decisions.title: Tasks, not just chat
decisions.body: The assistant is aimed at concrete jobs people already do, so its usefulness is easy to judge.

tradeoffs: An assistant that tries to answer everything is less trustworthy than one that knows when to hand over to a person.
outcomes: Reported internally as reducing support demand by around 40%. This is an operational estimate, not a controlled measurement.

featured.name: Excess Stock and Consignment
featured.summary: Visibility and workflow for surplus component stock, from bulk import to consignment and purchase orders.
featured.problem: Surplus stock is valuable only if the right people can see it. Stock lists arrive as large, inconsistent files, and consignment partners need their own view of what is held, sold and owed.
responsibilities: Import pipeline for large stock files
featured.solution: A platform that ingests large stock files, normalises them into a single searchable inventory and exposes it to sales teams and consignment partners. Consignees get a portal for their own stock, purchase orders are processed automatically, and quoting supports multiple currencies. AI-assisted classification helps fill in part details such as tariff codes and countries of origin.

decisions.title: Built for large imports
decisions.body: Import, validation and storage are designed around files of more than 100,000 records rather than the small ones that are easy to test.

decisions.title: Separate views for separate parties
decisions.body: Consignees see their own stock and workflows through a dedicated portal, keeping commercial data properly partitioned.

tradeoffs: Accepting messy real-world files means more validation and clearer error reporting, rather than asking suppliers to change formats.
outcomes: Handles stock imports of more than 100,000 records
Automated purchase-order processing for consignment workflows
Better commercial visibility of surplus stock

featured.name: Rama AI API
featured.summary: A provider-agnostic layer that lets applications use AI models without being tied to any one vendor.
featured.problem: When every application talks to a model provider directly, each one inherits that provider's SDK, request format and quirks. Switching providers, or simply comparing them, turns into a rewrite.
featured.solution: Applications call one internal API with a common request and response shape. Behind it, an adapter for each provider handles the details, so a model can be swapped or compared without changing the applications that use it.

decisions.title: One interface, many adapters
decisions.body: Provider-specific code lives in one place. Applications depend on the abstraction, not the vendor.

decisions.title: Built for experiments
decisions.body: The same request can be sent to different providers, which makes comparing models a configuration change rather than a project.

tradeoffs: A common interface can hide useful provider-specific features, so the design needs deliberate escape hatches.
outcomes: A reusable foundation for AI features and experiments across internal applications
Less provider-specific coupling in application code
